t051.sum: Faith is a living trust in God and in spiritual values, distinct from belief, which merely accepts a doctrine as true. Belief becomes faith only when it actually guides and shapes life, and faith transforms the philosophic God of probability into the God of experiential certainty. Faith is the price of entrance into the family of God and the key to Havona, and Jesus lived out its highest example.
t051.s1.i1: Accepting a teaching as true is only belief; belief becomes faith when it actually dominates the mode of living.
t051.s1.i3: Beliefs may become group possessions, but faith must always be personal.
t051.s1.i4: Faith is a God-knowing and man-serving life, a living experience concerned with spiritual meanings and supreme values.
t051.s2.i1: Faith transforms the philosophic God of probability into the saving God of certainty in personal religious experience.
t051.s2.i3: In science God is a possibility and in philosophy a probability, but in religion he is a certainty.
t051.s2.i4: God is not revealed by miracles or material proofs; he is known by trusting him.
t051.s2.i5: The more one knows of science, the less sure one becomes; the more religion one has, the more certain one is.
t051.s3.i1: True faith trusts in the goodness of God even amid bitter disappointment and defeat, and it generates profound courage in the face of calamity.
t051.s3.i2: Faith maintains an inexplicable poise and serenity in the midst of illness and suffering, abuse and injustice.
t051.s3.i3: True faith worships God in every circumstance and declares, "Though he slay me, yet will I serve him."
t051.s3.i4: Faith does not violate intellectual honesty, foster intolerance and persecution, or turn away from scientific discoveries.
t051.s3.i5: Faith vitalizes religion and moves the religionist to live the golden rule heroically.
t051.s4.i1: Faith links moral consciousness with the spiritual concept of enduring reality, making religion a technique of salvation.
t051.s4.i2: Faith is the price of entrance into the family of God, and forgiveness is the act of God in accepting that faith.
t051.s4.i3: Faith releases the divine spark that lives within man, the potential of eternal survival.
t051.s4.i4: The Adjuster's success in achieving survival depends less on theories of belief than on decisions, determinations, and steadfast faith.
t051.s5.i1: Jesus did not use faith as a consolation in suffering or a comfort in despair; he enjoyed serenity in an unquestioning trust in God.
t051.s5.i2: Jesus' great contribution was less a new idea of God than the human demonstration of a new and higher type of living faith.
t051.s5.i3: Jesus asks people not so much to believe in him as to believe with him, to believe as he believed.
t051.s5.i4: Jesus taught that simple, childlike faith is the key that opens the door of the kingdom.
t052.sum: Prayer is a personal and spontaneous expression of the attitude of the soul toward the spirit, the breath of the soul in the communion of sonship with God. Beginning as primitive petitions for material things, prayer gradually evolved into ethical and spiritual communion. Prayer does not change God but changes the one who prays, and it is truest when it seeks values, not things, and growth, not gratification. Jesus lived a life dedicated in prayer to the Father's will.
t052.s1.i2: Prayer is the communion of sonship and the expression of fellowship; the ideal prayer is spiritual communion leading to intelligent worship.
t052.s1.i3: Prayer is the breath of the soul, leading one to strive persistently to ascertain the Father's will.
t052.s1.i4: Prayer is the process of exchanging the human will for the divine will, part of the divine plan for making over what is into what ought to be.
t052.s1.i5: True prayer is the sincere and trusting communication of the creature's spiritual nature with the omnipresent spirit of the Creator.
t052.s2.i1: Primitive man prayed for material blessings such as food and rain; this was a perversion of prayer, yet it also stimulated social and ethical effort.
t052.s2.i2: Prayer is a monologue only in the most primitive minds; it soon becomes a dialogue and broadens into group worship.
t052.s2.i3: Magic was an attempt to adjust Deity to conditions; prayer is an effort to adjust the personality to the will of Deity.
t052.s2.i4: The idea of sacrifice, offering material things in place of the will, diminishes the efficacy of true prayer.
t052.s3.i1: Selfish and materialistic prayer is incompatible with ethical religion founded on unselfish love.
t052.s3.i3: Do not be so lazy as to ask God to solve problems for you; ask for wisdom and strength while you face them.
t052.s3.i5: God answers the attitude of the soul, not words, and he answers prayer with an enlarged revelation of truth, beauty, and goodness.
t052.s3.i6: Effective prayer requires courageously facing reality, sincere effort, choosing and carrying out the divine will, and living faith.
t052.s4.i1: Prayer does not change God, but great and lasting changes take place in the one who prays in faith.
t052.s4.i3: As a bird must spread its wings to ride rising air currents, prayer lifts one up on the spiritual currents of the universe.
t052.s4.i4: The quickest way to overcome the habit of criticizing a friend is to pray for him every day.
t052.s4.i5: Prayer offered sincerely in faith, even a foolish petition, never fails to enlarge the soul's capacity for spiritual receptivity.
t052.s5.i1: When one is wholly dedicated to doing the Father's will, every petition is answered, because the prayer is in accord with that will.
t052.s5.i2: Jesus prayed more for the spiritual progress of his brothers than for himself, and he urged prayer especially for enemies and persecutors.
t052.s5.i3: One should be able to talk with the Father as a son not only in times of distress but also when the soul is at peace.
t052.s5.i4: Jesus taught that after praying one should wait in silence for a time, giving the indwelling spirit opportunity to speak to the soul.
t052.s5.i5: Jesus usually prayed in the plural rather than the singular, and he prayed for himself only in the great crises of his earth life.
t052.s5.i6: For Jesus prayer was not a religious duty but a sincere expression of spiritual attitude and constant communion with God.
t053.sum: Worship is the act of recognizing and rejoicing in the intimate relationship with the Creator; it is the highest privilege and the first duty of all intelligent beings. Unlike prayer, which contains an element of self-interest, worship asks nothing and adores God for what he is. The worship impulse, beginning in primitive nature worship, was turned by the adjutant spirits toward the God of nature, and on Paradise it becomes the highest delight.
t053.s1.i2: Worship is the conscious and joyous recognition of the intimate and personal relationships of the Creators with their creatures.
t053.s1.i3: In the highest sense, worship is directed, directly or indirectly, to the Universal Father.
t053.s1.i4: Worship is personal communion with that which is divinely real, the source of reality, not a vain monologue.
t053.s1.i5: Worship is the act of the part identifying itself with the Whole, the finite with the Infinite, the son with the Father.
t053.s2.i2: True worship requests nothing and expects no reward; it is a natural response to the Father's lovable nature.
t053.s2.i3: When self-interest enters worship, it turns into prayer.
t053.s2.i5: Prayer is spiritually sustaining, but worship is divinely creative; prayer enriches life, and worship illuminates destiny.
t053.s2.i6: Modern religions have overemphasized prayer and neglected the more essential communion of worship.
t053.s3.i1: Sincere worship is the mobilization of all the powers of the personality under the leadership of the evolving soul and the direction of the Adjuster.
t053.s3.i2: The mortal mind consents to worship, the soul craves it, and the Adjuster conducts that worship to the Father.
t053.s3.i3: The fragments of the Father are empowered to register the genuine adoration of their subjects before the Universal Father.
t053.s3.i4: The Father's spirit speaks best when the human mind is in an attitude of true worship.
t053.s4.i1: Primitive man, fearing the incomprehensible forces of nature, worshiped almost everything on earth and in the heavens.
t053.s4.i2: The spirit of worship, the sixth adjutant spirit, constantly stimulated the worship urge in the primitive mind.
t053.s4.i3: The spirit of worship is the mark of spiritual-ascension candidacy, separating beings capable of possessing souls from those who are not.
t053.s4.i4: When the spirit of wisdom guides the worship impulse, man begins to turn from the objects of nature to the God of nature.
t053.s5.i1: Worship, or spiritual contemplation, must alternate with service, which keeps contact with material reality.
t053.s5.i3: Worship is effortless attention, the true rest of the soul, a form of restful spiritual activity.
t053.s5.i4: In time, thought leads to wisdom, and wisdom leads to worship.
t053.s5.i5: On Paradise worship is the highest delight and a refreshing play, and all the arts are employed in worship.
t053.s5.i6: On the seventh mansion world the ascender begins a new and more spiritual worship of the invisible Father.
t054.sum: Religious experience is the personal experience of living knowledge of God and supreme values under the guidance of the indwelling spirit. It is neither a reasoned system of belief nor a mystic ecstasy; it sprouts from moral consciousness and grows through faith and insight. However erroneous one's theology, the experience itself can be genuine, and its certainty cannot be refuted. Religious experience culminates in a certain consciousness of God and assurance of survival.
t054.s1.i1: True religion is neither a philosophic system proved by reason nor a mystic ecstasy enjoyed by a favored few.
t054.s1.i3: Religion is not the search for new facts but the discovery of new spiritual meanings in facts already known.
t054.s1.i4: The religious tendency is innate and universal; it is fostered by the spirit of worship and censored by the spirit of wisdom.
t054.s1.i5: The experience of realizing spiritual values is superideational and hard to express in human language; it is called God-consciousness.
t054.s2.i1: Every person early experiences conflict between selfish and altruistic urges, and in its resolution may first experience God-consciousness.
t054.s2.i2: When a moral being makes an unselfish choice against the urge to be selfish, that is primitive religious experience.
t054.s2.i3: It is right to identify altruistic desire with an influence outside oneself, with God, for it comes from the indwelling Adjuster.
t054.s2.i4: Religious "birth" is usually gradual, though there is a day of spirit rebirth; those who grow without crisis and those who pass through crisis should not disparage one another.
t054.s3.i1: Religious growth moves from stagnation to adjustment, from insecurity to faith, and from the bondage of fear to the liberty of sonship.
t054.s3.i2: God-consciousness may grow gradually or arrive in a dramatic moment, as with Paul on the Damascus road.
t054.s3.i4: Rather than seeking conversion, living faith, sincere worship, and unselfish prayer are a better way of approach to the Adjuster.
t054.s3.i5: Trances and visions should not be sought as religious experience, and Jesus never resorted to such methods.
t054.s4.i1: Religion begins with the quest for values, and systems of interpretive belief come later, so people agree more readily on values than on creeds.
t054.s4.i4: Knowing the varied religious experiences of others keeps one's own religion from becoming selfish and narrow.
t054.s5.i1: True religion is a living love and a life of service; it takes nothing away from a person and adds new meaning to all of life.
t054.s5.i2: A remarkable trait of the religious life is a peace that passes all understanding, unshaken by any disappointment.
t054.s5.i3: Religion rests on the Adjuster-derived postulate that God is knowable and attainable.
t054.s5.i4: The reality of religious experience is proportional to its spiritual content; its certainties are unassailable and its devotion beyond question.
t054.s5.i5: Religious experience culminates in a sure consciousness of God and an unquestioned assurance of the survival of the believer.
t055.sum: Personal religion is the "religion of the spirit," in which each person discovers and experiences God within his own soul, unlike the "religion of the mind," which leans on tradition and ecclesiastical authority. It cannot be received, borrowed, or learned from others; it grows with loyalty to supreme values. Jesus proclaimed this religion of living personal experience beyond the religion of authority, and its fruits appear in love and service.
t055.s1.h: Religion of the Mind and Religion of the Spirit
t055.s1.i1: There is the primitive religion of fear, the religion of civilization based on traditional authority, and the religion of revelation validated in human experience.
t055.s1.i3: The religion of authority offers an easy refuge to fearful and uncertain souls, but it demands only passive, intellectual assent.
t055.s1.i5: The religion of the mind ties one to the past, but the religion of the spirit, through progressive revelation, ever beckons to higher attainment.
t055.s2.i1: The greatest discovery a human soul can make is to find God for itself within itself and to live that as personal experience.
t055.s2.i2: It is good to revere the God-knowing leaders of the past, but not at the cost of sacrificing one's own experience of knowing God.
t055.s2.i3: Do not seek the word of God only in ancient records; the one born of the spirit discerns the word of God wherever it comes from.
t055.s2.i4: Once one begins to find God in one's soul, one soon finds him in the souls of others and in all creation.
t055.s2.i5: The religion of the apostles was to be not a theological refuge from fear but a real experience testifying that God had found and exalted them.
t055.s3.h: A Religion That Cannot Be Given
t055.s3.i2: Every child should be given the opportunity to grow his own religious experience; an adult's finished experience should not be forced upon him.
t055.s3.i3: Children are permanently impressed only by the loyalties of the adults with whom they live.
t055.s3.i5: Some people are too busy to grow; the chief obstacles to growth are prejudice and ignorance.
t055.s4.i1: Spiritual development depends on maintaining a living connection with true spiritual forces and bearing fruit by passing on to fellows what has been received.
t055.s4.i2: Spirituality measures both nearness to God and usefulness to fellows, and it grows as the selfish qualities of love are eliminated.
t055.s4.i3: Habits such as sensitivity to divine values, reflective meditation, and worshipful problem solving favor religious growth.
t055.s4.i4: Even when floods of adversity and hatred sweep over, the God-knowing person has a citadel of the spirit that is never assailed.
t055.s5.i1: The religions of authority divide people, but the religion of the spirit binds them together in unity of experience and destiny while allowing diversity of belief.
t055.s5.i2: The unity and brotherhood of mankind can be achieved only through the religion of personal spiritual experience.
t055.s5.i3: The evidence of knowing God is the fruit of the spirit borne in daily life and a life plan that stakes everything on the adventure of survival.
t055.s5.i4: The religion of the kingdom is personal, but its fruits are familial and social; no one can keep it within himself alone.
t055.s5.i5: The Father responds to the faintest flicker of faith, but those who are called must believe with body, mind, and spirit.
t056.sum: Institutional religion is the church and religious organization formed as individual religious experiences gather socially. It is natural for religious groups to arise when people share their faith, and such groups have practical value in fostering worship, education, and fellowship. But the more religion is institutionalized, the weaker its power for good and the greater the dangers of dogmatism, sectarianism, and alliance with secular power. The Urantia Book regards the church's displacement of Jesus' spiritual kingdom as a tragedy.
t056.s1.i1: Religion is the personal experience of knowing God as Father, but it leads to recognizing men as brothers, and so it has a social side.
t056.s1.i2: When people share their religious beliefs, some form of religious group with common goals inevitably arises.
t056.s1.i3: The purpose of the religious group is to dramatize loyalty, enlarge the attractions of truth, beauty, and goodness, and foster fellowship, the home, religious education, and group worship.
t056.s1.i4: Prayer sooner or later becomes a technique for institutionalizing every religion, giving rise to secondary agencies such as priests, scriptures, and rituals.
t056.s2.i4: The dangers of formalized religion include fixation of beliefs, fossilization of truth, diversion from the service of God to the service of the church, and oppressive authority.
t056.s3.i1: Institutionalized religion has become part of the social order that must be reconstructed, and so it cannot lead the coming social reconstruction.
t056.s3.i2: Religionists should take part in social and political life as individuals, not as groups; a religious group acting politically becomes a party or an economic organization.
t056.s3.i3: Early Christianity was free from all civil and economic entanglements, but later institutional Christianity became part of the structure of Western civilization.
t056.s3.i4: To be free from secular alliances, religion needs a critical philosophy, political and economic independence, loving fellowship, and a scientific attitude.
t056.s3.i5: Religious peace will not come until all religions renounce ecclesiastical authority and claims of spiritual sovereignty; God alone is spiritual sovereign.
t056.s4.i1: The religion of traditional authority offers an easy refuge to fearful souls, but at the price of spiritual and religious liberty.
t056.s4.i2: The religions of authority divide people by demanding uniformity of belief, while the religion of the spirit requires only unity of experience.
t056.s4.i3: True religion is not slavish belief in threats of punishment or in promises of mystical rewards.
t056.s4.i4: Jesus did not ask people to recite formulated creeds; he asked them to gather and share a supper in remembrance of his life.
t056.s5.h: The Church and the Kingdom of Heaven
t056.s5.i1: The rise of the church was itself natural and desirable; the trouble was that it almost wholly displaced Jesus' concept of the kingdom.
t056.s5.i2: A formal, institutionalized church came to take the place of the kingdom brotherhood of spirit-led individuals.
t056.s5.i3: Church membership does not mean kingdom fellowship; the one is spiritual, the other mainly social.
t056.s5.i4: The present church is the larval stage of the thwarted spiritual kingdom, a cocoon carrying the kingdom through the material age.
t056.s5.i5: A church that worships the living God, affirms the brotherhood of man, and removes the pressure of creeds holds great hope.
t057.sum: Truth is a spirit-discerned living reality that goes beyond knowledge, which deals with facts, and wisdom, which deals with relationships, to deal with reality values. God is the first truth, and all truth issues from him. Truth cannot be confined in words or creeds but is defined only by living, and static truth is dead truth. The Spirit of Truth enables people to realize this living, growing truth, and truth is unified with beauty and goodness in God.
t057.s1.i2: Knowledge originates in science, wisdom in philosophy, and truth in the religious experience of spiritual living; truth deals with reality values.
t057.s1.i3: Knowledge is demonstrable, but truth is experienced; knowledge is a possession of the mind, truth an experience of the soul.
t057.s1.i4: God is the first truth and the last fact, so all truth takes origin in him.
t057.s1.i5: Truth is always a revelation: autorevelation when it comes through the work of the Adjuster, epochal revelation when presented by celestial agencies.
t057.s2.i1: Physical facts are uniform, but truth is a living and flexible factor in the philosophy of the universe.
t057.s2.i2: Truth cannot be imprisoned in formulas, codes, or creeds; when one attempts to formulate it, it speedily dies.
t057.s2.i4: Truth is unshaken by shocks and free from all temporal fluctuations, yet it is never formalized and is always vital.
t057.s2.i5: It is folly to regard the past as the only source of truth, for truth lives always in the present and finds new expression in each generation.
t057.s3.i1: Truth cannot become man's possession without faith, for a person's thoughts and ideals can never rise higher than his faith.
t057.s3.i3: Fearing the unknown, man tends to fixate science, formalize philosophy, and dogmatize truth.
t057.s3.i4: There is never conflict between true knowledge and truth; conflict arises between knowledge and human beliefs colored by prejudice and fear.
t057.s3.i5: The more one knows truth and the more one becomes truth, the more one can understand the past and grasp the future.
t057.s4.i1: The Spirit of Truth is not the letter or law of truth but the conviction of true meanings on real spirit levels, a living and growing teacher.
t057.s4.i2: The God-knowing person lifts wisdom to the level of living truth, but the spiritually unprogressive soul drags living truth down to dead wisdom.
t057.s4.i3: Even the golden rule remains a mere ethical rule without the insight of the Spirit of Truth; its meaning is realized only by living it.
t057.s4.i4: Truth, the understanding of cosmic relationships and spiritual values, is best attained through the ministry of the Spirit of Truth.
t057.s5.i2: Because truth can be acted upon and lived, happiness follows the recognition of truth, while disappointment and sorrow follow error.
t057.s5.i3: All truth, whether material, philosophic, or spiritual, is both beautiful and good.
t057.s5.i4: Truth is coherent, beauty attractive, and goodness stabilizing; when these are harmonized, they become a high love.
t057.s5.i5: Truth is the basis of science and philosophy and the intellectual foundation of religion.
t058.sum: Beauty, together with truth and goodness, is one of the three ways in which man comprehends divinity; it is the recognition of the harmonious unification of diverse realities. In the physical universe we see divine beauty, and its climax is the cosmic drama of man seeking God and God seeking man. Art and the appreciation of beauty become part of religion when they are linked with ethics and spiritual motivation, and Jesus valued the power of beauty to lead to worship.
t058.s1.i1: Creatures can comprehend divinity as truth, beauty, and goodness.
t058.s1.i2: In the physical universe one sees divine beauty, in the intellectual world one discerns truth, and goodness is found in religious experience.
t058.s1.i3: The Father enjoys the response of divine beauty that Havona presents and delights in providing the evolving universes with patterns of harmony.
t058.s1.i4: Even beauty and truth would be divorced from the hope of survival were they not attributes of a loving Father.
t058.s2.i1: Beauty, or art, is largely a matter of the unification of contrasts, and diversity is essential to the concept of beauty.
t058.s2.i2: Beauty is the intellectual recognition of the harmonious synthesis of the diversities of phenomenal reality, derived from eternal oneness.
t058.s2.i5: Universal beauty is the recognition of the reflection of the Isle of Paradise in the material creation.
t058.s3.i1: The climax of finite art is the drama of uniting the two poles of Creator and creature: man seeking God and God seeking man.
t058.s3.i3: The existence of beauty implies the presence of an appreciative creature mind.
t058.s3.i4: Cosmologic thinking is accompanied by curiosity toward harmony, aesthetic appreciation, and ethical sensitivity leading to God-consciousness.
t058.s4.i1: The search for beauty becomes part of religion only when it enriches ethical and moral concepts.
t058.s4.i3: The high mission of all art is to foreshadow higher reality and to crystallize the emotions of time into the thought of eternity.
t058.s4.i4: Art arises from the attempt to escape the lack of beauty in the material environment; it is a gesture toward the morontia level.
t058.s4.i5: If truth, beauty, and goodness are not unified in the experience of the artist or philosopher, the expression lacks a true soul.
t058.s4.i6: The celestial artists of the morontia worlds portray in art the divine beauty of the Paradise Creators.
t058.s5.i1: Viewing Flavius's art treasures, Jesus said there was no reason to condemn the appreciation of the beauty of things created by the Father and fashioned by man.
t058.s5.i2: Jesus taught that beauty has great value in leading to the worship impulse, especially in children.
t058.s5.i3: The spirit that Jesus and the Father send is not only the spirit of truth but also the spirit of idealistic beauty.
t058.s5.i4: The Hebrews based their religion on goodness and the Greeks on beauty, but the love Jesus revealed embraces truth, beauty, and goodness together.
t058.s5.i5: The beauty of divine love, once fully admitted to the human heart, forever destroys the charm of sin and the power of evil.
t059.sum: Goodness, together with truth and beauty, is one of the three ways of comprehending divinity, but it is understood only in relation to personality. God's primal perfection consists in the perfection of the goodness inherent in his nature, and that goodness is fully revealed only in personal religious experience. For man, goodness is always relative and growing, more a quest than a possession until Paradise is attained. The goodness of God leads people to repentance.
t059.s1.i3: God is supremely great and good, and greatness and goodness are inseparably one in him.
t059.s1.i4: The infinite goodness of the Father is beyond the finite mind's comprehension and is discerned only by contrast with relative imperfection.
t059.s1.i5: God the Supreme is truth, beauty, and goodness, for these concepts are the finite maximum of ideational experience.
t059.s2.i1: Truth and beauty may be conceived without personality, but divine goodness is understood only in relation to personality.
t059.s2.i2: The goodness of God is found only in the spiritual world of personal religious experience, and religion is essentially faith-trust in that goodness.
t059.s2.i4: Goodness is the mind's recognition of the relative values of the levels of divine perfection, and it implies a moral mind that discriminates between good and evil.
t059.s2.i5: Goodness embraces ethics, morality, and religion, the craving for experiential perfection.
t059.s3.i1: Good and evil are words denoting relative levels of human comprehension of the observable universe.
t059.s3.i2: One should not take social custom or religious tradition as the standard of goodness but choose the good by the spiritual standards set by the indwelling spirit.
t059.s3.i3: Experience is good when it heightens the appreciation of beauty, strengthens the moral will, and enlarges the capacity to love and serve one's fellows.
t059.s3.i5: As one ascends the universe scale, goodness increases and evil diminishes, and on Paradise goodness is no longer contrastive but perfect.
t059.s4.h: Goodness and the Possibility of Evil
t059.s4.i1: The possibility of evil is necessary to moral choosing, but actual evil need not exist.
t059.s4.i2: The presence of good and evil in the world is proof of the reality of personality, with a moral will that chooses between them.
t059.s4.i3: Spiritual evolution is an experience of increasingly choosing the good, with a corresponding decrease in the potential of evil.
t059.s4.i4: No good deed is ever wholly lost; it remains forever effective in proportion to the divinity of its motivation.
t059.s5.i2: Goodness without graciousness commands respect but repels affection; only when it is gracious is it universally attractive.
t059.s5.i3: Righteousness of conduct must be judged by motives, so the highest goodness is unconscious.
t059.s5.i4: An isolated morality that overemphasizes goodness while excluding truth and neglecting beauty fails to hold many modern minds.
t059.s5.i5: All true goodness, whether personal morality, social fairness, or divine ministry, is equally true and beautiful.
t060.sum: "God is love." In The Urantia Book love is the dominant characteristic of all God's personal dealings with his creatures, and it embraces truth, beauty, and goodness. The Father's love individualizes each person as an irreplaceable child and dwells within man through the Adjuster. Love is the desire to do good to others; it cannot be held captive and becomes real only when bestowed upon one's fellows. Jesus gave the new commandment to love one another "as I have loved you."
t060.s1.i1: Because God is love, his only personal attitude toward the affairs of the universe is always a reaction of divine affection.
t060.s1.i2: The love of God is not induced by sacrifice or intercession; the Father himself loves us.
t060.s1.i4: The love of God is a farseeing parental affection that functions in unity with wisdom and sometimes includes discipline for our good.
t060.s1.i5: Love is the dominant characteristic of all God's personal dealings with his creatures.
t060.s2.i1: The Father's love individualizes each personality as a unique child, eternally irreplaceable.
t060.s2.i2: The greatest manifestation of divine love for mortals is the bestowal of the Adjusters, and its greatest revelation is the bestowal life of Michael.
t060.s2.i3: The love and devotion an Adjuster gives to its subject is the most truly divine affection in all creation.
t060.s2.i4: God is love and the Son is mercy; mercy is applied love, love in action.
t060.s2.i5: We love God because we discern that he truly loves us; the experience of loving is a response to the experience of being loved.
t060.s3.i2: In its true sense, love, whether human or divine, connotes the mutual regard of whole personalities.
t060.s3.i4: Love is born only of thoroughgoing understanding of a neighbor's motives and sentiments; one cannot love fellows by mere willpower.
t060.s3.i5: Love must continually readapt its concept of the highest good of the one loved, under the guidance of the Spirit of Truth.
t060.s4.i1: All true love is from God, and man receives the divine affection as he bestows that love upon his neighbors.
t060.s4.i3: The circuit of love proceeds from the Father, through sons to brothers, and thence to the Supreme.
t060.s4.i4: Love is the soil of religious growth; love is the essence of religion and the wellspring of superior civilization.
t060.s5.i1: Jesus revealed a God of love, and that love embraces truth, beauty, and goodness.
t060.s5.i3: Beyond the commandment to love one's neighbor as oneself, Jesus gave the new commandment: "Love one another as I have loved you."
t060.s5.i4: The new commandment is not a new burden but a new joy of sharing affection with one's fellows, and the greatest love is to lay down one's life for one's friends.
t060.s5.i5: To share the Master's love is to share his service; that love does not make a new world but makes the old world new.
t060.s5.i6: Advanced mortals on worlds settled in light and life have learned that love is the greatest thing in the universe and know that God is love.
